column1: # dsh-os verb table - single source of truth for the atomic command surface.
#   verb        dotted verb, exactly as dispatched (group + '.' + subverb, or a bare top-level verb)
#   positionals '|'-separated positional parameter names in order; '-' when the verb takes none
#   flags       '|'-separated accepted flags (long form, no leading dashes); '-' when none
#   perm        R = read-only/query, never prompts; W = mutating, requires --allow
#   codes       '|'-separated error codes this verb can return, beyond the generic set
# Generic codes available to every verb: E_USAGE E_TYPE E_PERMISSION E_IO E_ABORTED E_INTERNAL

column1: # file.verify.* are assertions: they compare against a caller-supplied expectation and report the
# observed value alongside the match result. They never modify the target.
# system.* are pure queries, never privileged, and must degrade field-by-field rather than fail whole.
# task.* manage processes. task.launch is the "open this program/document" verb (command.txt wrote
# "lunch", which is a typo); it never launches through a shell string.
# service.* address OS service managers: Windows SCM, systemd, launchd. Start/stop/restart need
# elevation and must report E_ELEVATION_REQUIRED instead of failing opaquely.
# environment.* default to the user scope. A change to user or machine scope does not affect
# already-running processes; every mutating call reports the scope it actually wrote.
# An environment variable has attributes: PATH is one, as are PATHEXT, LIB and INCLUDE. A plain
# variable holds one string; an attribute holds an ordered list joined by the platform separator
# (';' on Windows, ':' on POSIX). Both levels expose the same five operations, so
# `environment get PATH` returns the raw string while `environment attr get PATH` returns the split
# entries. --attr selects the attribute name and defaults to PATH.
